title: Mata Ganga
hookLine: Guru Arjan's wife, who, tradition says, walked to Baba Buddha with simple bread and onions to ask for a son's blessing

lines: THE FIRST TIME: CARRIAGE AND FINE FOOD.
cards: What do you bring to someone whose blessing you want? One instinct is to bring the best: the good dishes, the nicest clothes, a little ceremony to show you mean it. That's exactly what Mata Ganga did the first time.
Tradition says she set out with attendants, a carriage and fine food, to visit an old man who lived out among the fields and cattle. She came home with nothing. The second time, she walked.

teach.b: Mata Ganga was the wife of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, Bibi Bhani's son. Tradition says that for a long time the couple had no child, and Mata Ganga longed for a son.
Guru Arjan, the story goes, sent her to Baba Buddha, the old Sikh who had known Guru Nanak and now tended the Guru's fields and herds.
So she went the way a Guru's wife might be expected to: carriage, servants, rich dishes, the dust of the procession rolling up the road.
Baba Buddha, tradition says, asked what all the commotion was about, and gave no blessing. She went home disappointed. Guru Arjan didn't scold her.
He suggested another way. This time she ground the flour and kneaded the dough herself.
She made plain bread, the kind farm workers eat, took onions and buttermilk with it, and went on foot, alone or nearly so. Baba Buddha was hungry from the work, and glad. He sat and ate.

teach.h: AN ONION CRUSHED IN HIS FIST.
teach.b: Then, tradition says, he crushed an onion in his fist and said her son would be strong enough to crush the pride of tyrants the same way.
Sikhs say the son born to her was Guru Hargobind, the Guru remembered for taking up the sword alongside the Name. So what changed? Not the request.
Not the person. Only how she came. With the carriage, she arrived as someone important.
With the bread, she arrived as someone asking. The story says the blessing waited for the second.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Mata Ganga's visit to Baba Buddha as a lesson in humility: the blessing came when she walked there with bread she had made herself.

o: Guru Arjan's wife, who walked with plain bread
Baba Buddha's daughter, who farmed his fields
Guru Hargobind's wife, who ran the langar

games.q: two visits, one blessing — tap the pairs.
p: on foot, with bread she made
a blessing for a strong son

s: Baba Buddha blessed Mata Ganga on her first visit
tradition says the first visit, with the carriage and fine food, brought no blessing.
on the second visit she made the bread herself
she ground the flour, kneaded the dough and carried it on foot.
Guru Arjan scolded her after the first visit
in the story he simply suggested another way to go.

games.q: you're Mata Ganga. your first visit, with a carriage and fine food, brought no blessing. what do you do next?
o: make plain bread yourself and walk there with it.
games.why: tradition says she went on foot with plain bread, onions and buttermilk, and Baba Buddha ate and blessed her.

practice: Bring to mind one person who could use something plain and warm today, a sandwich, a bowl of soup, tea in a flask, fruit you washed yourself, and let the picture be specific: what you'd carry, how you'd get there, where you'd set it down.
Notice any urge to make it fancier, and let it go; if you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Mata Ganga. Guru Arjan's wife and, Sikhs say, Guru Hargobind's mother, who went back to Baba Buddha on foot with bread she made herself.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Mata Ganga; Mata, mother, is a title of honor for the Gurus' wives.

carryVoice: Your line: simple bread, big blessing. It was how she came. Day eight hundred nine, done.
